Pond pasture · two flights, four days apart · fused

Two Sensors, One Pond

The multispectral camera measured how alive every square foot is. The laser measured how tall everything stands. Neither knows the whole story — so we laid one on top of the other, cell by cell, and asked both at once.

21.3 ac of fused coverage 2 instruments · 4 days apart 8 in fusion grid multispectral Aug 19 · LiDAR Aug 15, 2026

The idea

Condition × structure

Each instrument answers one question and is blind to the other. The plant-health camera sees a lush tree and a lush weed as the same green; the laser sees a dead tree and a living one as the same shape. Cross them and every patch of ground lands in a grid square that neither sensor could fill alone:

Both instruments, one image

Condition painted on structure

Plant-health color from the camera, draped over the laser's surface relief. Every crown is dimensional and graded; the pond reads flat red (water), rimmed by the greenest growth on the property.

The working map

The fuel-structure map

Every 8-inch cell classified by both answers at once. One height band matters enough to get its own colors: knee-high to head-high growth — what firefighters call ladder fuel, the rungs that can carry flame from the grass up into the crowns. This is the map the fire conversation — and the grazing plan — runs on.

11.2 ac
cured fine fuel — the herd's open-ground work
1.8 ac
tall & dry — the class only the fusion can see; field-check list below
0.6 ac
ladder-height vegetation (20 in–6½ ft), cured and green combined
23 ft
typical oak crown height — the water-loving (riparian) giants below the dam reach 80

One line through everything

An 810-foot walk, measured

A straight transect from the northwest grass, through the oak groves, across the pond, over the dam, and down into the riparian trees below it. The brown line is the laser's bare earth; the colored surface riding on top is everything standing on it, painted by the camera's health reading.

Same ground, three answers

Photo · condition · structure

The pond's southeast margin and dam, asked three different questions. This is the habit the fused map is built on — no single layer gets the final word.

Honest limits

Reading the fusion honestly

About the "tall & dry" class

Those brown fringes on the crowns are where the laser says tall and the camera says not green. Some of that is exactly what it sounds like — dead limbs and drought-stressed crown edges, the fuel worth a walk with a saw. Some of it is instrument disagreement: the flights were four days apart, crowns shade their own north edges, and the two maps can slip an inch or two against each other at a canopy's rim. Treat the brown as a field-check list, not a verdict — the map's job is to tell you where to walk, and 1.8 acres is a short walk.

  1. The layers were measured on different days. Aug 15 (laser) and Aug 19 (camera). Nothing grew meaningfully in four August days, but shadows and water level can shift at the margins.
  2. Heights are relative, not absolute. The two deliveries use different vertical references, so this page only ever subtracts heights within one instrument — height above ground is solid; absolute elevations between deliveries are not comparable.
  3. Grass below ankle height merges with the ground in the laser's view — the fine-fuel class leans on the camera, the ladder and canopy classes lean on the laser. That's the point of using both.
  4. Class edges are honest guesses. The 20-inch and 6½-foot breaks are chosen for the fire story (surface fuel vs. ladder vs. canopy), and cells near a boundary can sit on either side. The acreages are robust; any single cell is not.

What it's for

From map to plan

This fused map is the targeting layer the Goats vs. Fire brief runs on: the amber acres are open-ground herd work, the red and brown cells are where grazing gets paired with a saw crew, and the green margins are worth protecting on the way through. After the herd works the ground, both flights repeat and this page's maps get their after picture.

The full reading course for each instrument: Reading the Pond Flight (multispectral) and Reading the Bunkhouse LiDAR (laser).

TWO SENSORS, ONE POND · multispectral flown Aug 19, 2026 (Sentera, Pix4Dfields) · LiDAR flown Aug 15, 2026 (DJI, DJI Terra) · fused on a 0.2 m (8 in) grid over the flight overlap (21.3 valid acres), EPSG:32611
Classes: height from LiDAR DSM−DEM, breaks at 20 in and 6½ ft · condition from the camera's NDVI (green ≥ 0.50 in the tall band, ≥ 0.40 below it; bare < 0.15) · water by near-infrared + NDVI + height under 20 in. All numbers computed from the delivered files.
